question: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?

options.A: Log every update and deletion for later audit
options.B: Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
options.C: Restrict deletions to business hours
options.D: Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely

rationale: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (A) and confirmations (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (C) narrows the window without closing it.

question: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?

options.A: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
options.B: The model, which may have degraded overnight
options.C: The system prompt wording
options.D: The temperature setting

rationale: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (B), unchanged prompt (C), and sampling (D) do not correlate with the refresh.

question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

options.A: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
options.B: Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
options.C: One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors
options.D: Limit the platform to ten capabilities

rationale: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (D) sacrifices the requirement.

question: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

options.A: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents
options.B: One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
options.C: Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
options.D: A single fine-tuned model for both

rationale: Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (A) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

options.A: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general
options.B: Workflows always outperform agents
options.C: The team lacked time to build an agent
options.D: The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path

rationale: The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (A) and universal claims (B) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (C) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

question: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?

options.A: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
options.B: Ship and count complaints
options.C: Exact string match against one reference summary per clause
options.D: Grade outputs by length

rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (C) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (D) measures nothing.

question: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?

options.A: Roll it out; demos are representative
options.B: Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
options.C: Ask the team to vote
options.D: Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner

rationale: Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

question: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?

options.A: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
options.B: A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
options.C: A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary
options.D: Blocking free-text queries entirely

rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (A) is not a control, model instructions (B) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (D) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

question: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?

options.A: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap
options.B: Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
options.C: Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher
options.D: Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit

rationale: Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

question: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?

options.A: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
options.B: Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
options.C: Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
options.D: Let each engineer keep personal settings only

rationale: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

question: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

options.A: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
options.B: Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region
options.C: The Claude API with request logging disabled
options.D: Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit

rationale: A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (A), disabled logging (C), and transport encryption (D) all still involve the data leaving the account.

question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
options.B: Use the Claude API and replicate the controls
options.C: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
options.D: Let each team choose its own path

rationale: Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, replication (B) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance.

question: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?

options.A: It reduces token cost
options.B: It removes the need for evaluation
options.C: It guarantees lower latency
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place

rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (A) or remove the need to evaluate (B), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

question: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?

options.A: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously
options.B: Force the model to answer within two seconds
options.C: Increase the legacy timeout
options.D: Use the smallest model available

rationale: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, D) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (C) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

question: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?

options.A: Using identical prompts in both
options.B: Establishing which behaviors must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
options.C: Choosing the cheaper platform for both
options.D: Deploying to whichever region is nearest

rationale: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behavior, and cost (C) and proximity (D) do not address consistency.

question: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?

options.A: Which model to use
options.B: The expected token cost
options.C: Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person
options.D: Whether the agent can be built in the available time

rationale: Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (A), cost (B), and schedule (D) are all downstream of that boundary.

question: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?

options.A: The more capable design, since capability is the point
options.B: The design the team finds more interesting
options.C: The design with more components, for future flexibility
options.D: Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity

rationale: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.

question: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?

options.A: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.B: Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
options.C: Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator
options.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

rationale: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behavior cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (B), disclosure (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

question: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?

options.A: It uses more than one model
options.B: Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
options.C: It has an evaluation suite
options.D: It includes a human approval step

rationale: Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (A), evaluation (C), and approval steps (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

question: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?

options.A: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
options.B: Agreement from the engineering team
options.C: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
options.D: A completed cost estimate

rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (A), consensus (B), and cost (D) do not establish whether the system works.

question: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?

options.A: It gives a reliable measure of quality
options.B: It is acceptable if it is large enough
options.C: It only matters for regulated systems
options.D: It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter

rationale: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

question: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behavior. How is this best prevented?

options.A: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviors the system must not lose
options.B: Changing one thing at a time
options.C: Reviewing changes more carefully
options.D: Limiting how often prompts change

rationale: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (B) and careful review (C) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

question: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?

options.A: Only a reported incident
options.B: A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
options.C: A fixed annual schedule
options.D: A change in cost

rationale: Any change to the things that determine behavior invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (A) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (D) does not affect correctness.

question: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?

options.A: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence
options.B: Refuse, since logging creates risk
options.C: Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
options.D: Log responses only

rationale: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (A) and blanket refusal (B) ignore one side, and a partial rule (D) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

question: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?

options.A: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
options.B: It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
options.C: It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel
options.D: It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content

rationale: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (A) and prompt instructions (B) are bypassable, and transport security (C) says nothing about the content.

question: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?

options.A: The organization that deployed the workflow
options.B: The model provider
options.C: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.D: Nobody, since the output was automated

rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D).

question: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?

options.A: Provide the headline accuracy figure
options.B: Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated
options.C: Explain that quality cannot be summarised
options.D: Provide the model's benchmark score

rationale: A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark score (D) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (C) fails the sponsor.

question: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: The cost of additional licenses
options.B: The need for a larger model
options.C: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
options.D: The training schedule

rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licenses (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

question: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?

options.A: Full documentation at delivery
options.B: A longer warranty period
options.C: Training every user
options.D: A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update

rationale: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than drift.

question: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?

options.A: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
options.B: One model for everything, for simplicity
options.C: The largest model for everything, for safety
options.D: The newest model for everything

rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

question: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?

options.A: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
options.B: A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.C: A limit that only matters for long documents
options.D: A setting to raise when quality drops

rationale: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?

options.A: Appoint one team to own all prompting
options.B: Freeze the prompts
options.C: Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
options.D: Move all prompts into the system prompt

rationale: Prompts that determine production behavior deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (A) may not fit the organization, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and relocation (D) does not address governance.

question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?

options.A: A written policy circulated by email
options.B: A one-off training session
options.C: Requiring approval for each use
options.D: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code

rationale: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (C) creates friction without conveying practice.

question: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement program is working?

options.A: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
options.B: The number of people trained
options.C: License utilization
options.D: The volume of tool calls

rationale: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilization (C), and activity (D) measure uptake rather than benefit.

question: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?

options.A: Whether the team needs more training
options.B: Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
options.C: Whether a larger model would help
options.D: Whether the legacy service should be rewritten

rationale: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalog that changes daily. Which architecture fits?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the catalog nightly
options.B: Load the catalog into the system prompt
options.C: Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalog changes, with the model answering from retrieved context
options.D: An autonomous agent that browses the public website

rationale: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?

options.A: The generation prompt
options.B: The model version
options.C: The user interface
options.D: Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently

rationale: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

options.A: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
options.B: Shorten all tool descriptions
options.C: Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
options.D: Replace the agent with a larger model

rationale: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?

options.A: Exact match against reference summaries
options.B: A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
options.C: Average output length compared to references
options.D: User thumbs-up counts alone

rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?

options.A: Ship it and monitor complaints
options.B: Team vote followed by rollout
options.C: Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
options.D: Rollout with a feedback form

rationale: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?

options.A: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
options.B: A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
options.C: Restricting the feature to structured queries only
options.D: A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing

rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?

options.A: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
options.B: Review every output regardless of risk
options.C: Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
options.D: Review only what users complain about

rationale: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?

options.A: The highest observed number
options.B: Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review
options.C: A refusal to quantify
options.D: An average weighted to look favorable

rationale: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?

options.A: Response latency targets
options.B: The choice of programming language
options.C: Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
options.D: The number of model providers

rationale: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?

options.A: Workflows are always more accurate
options.B: Agents cannot process documents
options.C: Workflows use less context
options.D: The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable

rationale: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?

options.A: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
options.B: Splitting the preamble across two requests
options.C: Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
options.D: Moving the preamble into a few-shot block

rationale: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?

options.A: The final design only
options.B: The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
options.C: The team members involved
options.D: The implementation timeline

rationale: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?

options.A: Final outputs only
options.B: Aggregate latency metrics only
options.C: Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
options.D: User feedback only

rationale: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?

options.A: A recorded walkthrough
options.B: A shared chat channel
options.C: Individual coaching sessions
options.D: Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow

rationale: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?

options.A: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
options.B: Logging modifications for later review
options.C: Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
options.D: Running the agent during business hours only

rationale: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it

question: A client requires that inference run inside their own AWS account. What does this determine?

options.A: The model family only
options.B: That a data processing agreement is sufficient
options.C: Deployment through Amazon Bedrock in the client's account and region
options.D: That request logging must be disabled

rationale: Running inside the client's own cloud boundary is what the requirement describes. A contract (B) and logging settings (D) do not keep the data in the account, and the model family (A) is a separate choice

question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud wants identity and audit handled by existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
options.B: Use the Claude API and rebuild the controls
options.C: Use Bedrock for feature parity
options.D: Let each team decide

rationale: Aligning with the governed platform makes existing controls apply without duplication. Rebuilding (B) drifts, a different cloud (C) creates a second control plane, and per-team choice (D) removes governance

question: What is the main architectural benefit of routing all model traffic through one internal service?

options.A: Lower token prices
options.B: It removes the need for evaluation
options.C: It guarantees lower latency
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are applied consistently in one place

rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once. It does not change unit price (A), remove evaluation (B), or reduce latency (C)

question: Two designs both satisfy the requirement; one is materially simpler. What decides?

options.A: The more capable design, since headroom is valuable
options.B: Whether any stated requirement needs the extra capability, against the ongoing cost of complexity
options.C: Whichever the team prefers to build
options.D: The one with more components, for flexibility

rationale: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Headroom (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (D) pay that cost without justification

question: A required compliance control depends on the model behaving correctly. What is the correct judgment?

options.A: Acceptable if measured accuracy is very high
options.B: Not acceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.C: Acceptable with a documented residual risk
options.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

rationale: A control that must hold needs a guarantee, which probabilistic behavior cannot supply. High accuracy (A), documentation (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee

question: Where should the boundary of automation be drawn in a solution that makes customer-affecting decisions?

options.A: Wherever the model performs well in testing
options.B: As far as the budget allows
options.C: At whatever the client requests
options.D: Where accountability for the decision sits, keeping those decisions with a person

rationale: Accountability determines what may be automated at all, and that boundary is an architectural decision. Test performance (A), budget (B), and unexamined requests (C) do not address responsibility

question: What must exist before a solution is declared production-ready?

options.A: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
options.B: A successful demonstration
options.C: Sign-off from the engineering team
options.D: A completed cost model

rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar. A demonstration (B), consensus (C), and cost (D) do not establish whether it works

question: An evaluation set contains only cases the system already handles. What is the effect?

options.A: It provides a reliable quality measure
options.B: It is fine if it is large
options.C: It overstates performance and conceals the failures that matter
options.D: It matters only in regulated contexts

rationale: An unrepresentative sample measures the wrong distribution, and size does not correct bias. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix it (B), and the problem is general (D)

question: How should a request to log every prompt and response for audit be handled?

options.A: Implement it, since audit takes precedence
options.B: Decline, because logging creates risk
options.C: Log responses but not prompts
options.D: Establish what the audit requires, because prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data

rationale: Audit and data protection are both real, and the design must serve the audit purpose without retaining more than warranted. Blanket action (A) or refusal (B) ignores one side, and an arbitrary split (C) is unjustified

question: Who is accountable when an automated Claude workflow produces a harmful decision?

options.A: The model provider
options.B: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.C: The organization that deployed it
options.D: No one, because the decision was automated

rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes. The provider (A) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D)

question: A sponsor asks for one number that shows whether the solution is working. What is the right response?

options.A: Give the headline accuracy figure
options.B: Give the measure tied to the decision they face, and state what it does not cover
options.C: Explain that this cannot be reduced to a number
options.D: Give the model's benchmark score

rationale: A useful metric matches the decision and is honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark (D) can mislead, and refusing (C) fails the sponsor

question: A ten-user pilot is about to expand to two thousand users. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
options.B: License cost
options.C: Whether a larger model is needed
options.D: The training rollout plan

rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and surfacing those is the architect's contribution. Cost (B), model size (C), and training (D) follow from knowing what breaks

question: How should a model be chosen for a solution containing several distinct tasks?

options.A: Match each task to the smallest model meeting its requirement, and evaluate the choices
options.B: One model everywhere, for simplicity
options.C: The largest model everywhere, for safety
options.D: The newest model everywhere

rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate on evidence. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit

question: How should the context window be treated in a production design?

options.A: As capacity to fill as completely as possible
options.B: As a budget allocated deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.C: As a concern only for long documents
options.D: As a setting to increase whenever quality drops

rationale: Context is scarce and its allocation drives quality, so it is designed. Filling it (A) dilutes, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix allocation

question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across dozens of repositories. What is most durable?

options.A: A policy document circulated once
options.B: A single training session
options.C: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
options.D: Requiring approval for every use

rationale: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (D) adds friction without conveying practice

question: A client will not accept a solution whose behavior cannot be explained to their auditor. What does this constrain?

options.A: The model family only
options.B: The cost model
options.C: The architecture, which must make decisions traceable and the controls inspectable
options.D: The deployment region

rationale: Auditability is an architectural property covering tracing and inspectable controls. Model family (A), cost (B), and region (D) do not by themselves make behavior explicable

question: What is the main risk of building directly against a single cloud's model service with no abstraction?

options.A: Moving later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
options.B: Higher token cost
options.C: Lower accuracy
options.D: Slower responses

rationale: Coupling determines the cost of change, which is the architectural concern. Cost (B), accuracy (C), and latency (D) are not consequences of the coupling itself

question: A solution must serve users in two regions with different data residency rules. What follows?

options.A: One deployment in the cheaper region
options.B: A single deployment with encryption in transit
options.C: Whichever region has the lowest latency
options.D: Separate deployments whose data stays within each region's boundary

rationale: Residency is satisfied by keeping the data within each boundary. A single deployment (A, B) moves data across it, and latency (C) does not address the rule

question: A requirement is stated as make it as accurate as possible. What should the architect do?

options.A: Choose the largest model and optimise from there
options.B: Establish the accuracy the use case actually needs and what an error costs
options.C: Build the most complex design the budget allows
options.D: Defer the question until after the pilot

rationale: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be made concrete. Defaulting to maximum capability (A, C) spends without a target, and deferring (D) leaves the design unanchored

question: Two components each work correctly but the system fails intermittently at their boundary. What does this suggest?

options.A: One component needs a larger model
options.B: The contract between them is underspecified, particularly for edge and error cases
options.C: The system needs more components
options.D: The failure is transient and can be retried

rationale: Boundary failures between correct components point at the contract. Capability (A) and more components (C) do not define the interface, and retrying (D) hides it

question: A design proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely. What should the architect raise?

options.A: Nothing, retention is always safer
options.B: That storage is expensive
options.C: That it will slow the system
options.D: Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations retention creates

rationale: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it. Treating retention as free of risk (A) is the error, and cost (B) and speed (C) are minor by comparison

question: How should a solution handle the case where the model is confident and wrong?

options.A: Design so that consequential outputs are verified against something independent of the model
options.B: Trust the confidence signal
options.C: Ask the model to double-check
options.D: Use two models and take the agreement

rationale: Independence is what catches confident error. Confidence (B) is not evidence, self-checking (C) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (D)

question: An evaluation shows 94% accuracy. What else must be known before this is actionable?

options.A: The model version only
options.B: The token cost of the evaluation
options.C: What the 6% look like, and what each failure costs
options.D: How long the evaluation took

rationale: A headline rate is only meaningful alongside the shape and cost of the failures. Version (A), cost (B), and duration (D) do not describe the risk

question: What should happen when a model version is updated beneath a production solution?

options.A: Nothing, versions are compatible
options.B: Increase monitoring for a week
options.C: Roll back automatically if complaints rise
options.D: Re-run the evaluation suite before the change reaches production traffic

rationale: A change to the thing that determines behavior invalidates prior measurement. Assuming compatibility (A) is unsafe, and monitoring (B) or reacting to complaints (C) detects after users are affected

question: A stakeholder asks why the solution cannot simply be fully automated. What is the most useful answer?

options.A: That the technology is not ready
options.B: That automation is always risky
options.C: Which specific decisions carry accountability or are unverifiable, and what automating them would risk
options.D: That the budget does not allow it

rationale: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited. Generic claims about readiness (A) or risk (B) are not, and budget (D) is not the reason

question: What should be handed over with a solution so it survives its first year?

options.A: The source code
options.B: The evaluation suite, the criteria, the owner, and the routine for re-checking
options.C: A recorded demonstration
options.D: A list of prompts used

rationale: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain, with someone responsible. Code (A), a demonstration (C), and prompts (D) are artefacts without the means to verify them

question: A team reports the solution has become worse, but nothing was deployed. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The inputs or the surrounding usage changed
options.B: The model degraded on its own
options.C: The prompts wore out
options.D: The evaluation was wrong originally

rationale: Behavior changes with what is fed to it, and distribution drift is the usual cause. Models do not degrade unprompted (B), prompts do not wear out (C), and the original evaluation is not the first suspect (D)

question: How should prompts that determine production behavior be managed?

options.A: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on change, like code
options.B: Edited in place when someone notices a problem
options.C: Kept in a shared document for easy editing
options.D: Frozen after launch

rationale: Anything that determines production behavior needs the lifecycle of code. Ad hoc edits (B) and open documents (C) invite unreviewed change, and freezing (D) blocks improvement

question: An organization asks how to measure whether Claude Code is worth the license cost. What should be measured?

options.A: Number of tool invocations
options.B: Change in the delivery outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
options.C: Number of users onboarded
options.D: Hours spent in the tool

rationale: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated. Invocations (A), onboarding (C), and time in tool (D) measure usage rather than benefit

question: What most often blocks a team from getting good results from Claude Code on an existing codebase?

options.A: The size of the repository
options.B: The programming language
options.C: The absence of committed context describing the conventions and structure
options.D: The number of contributors

rationale: Missing project context is the usual cause, and it is the one the team can fix. Size (A), language (B), and contributor count (D) do not by themselves prevent good results

question: A team exposes a customer-support agent that can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds, and delete user accounts. Support staff only ever need to read tickets and draft replies. Applying least-privilege principles, which change best reduces risk?

options.A: Add logging to the refund and delete tools so misuse can be audited later.
options.B: Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration entirely.
options.C: Keep all tools but add a confirmation prompt before refunds and deletions.
options.D: Replace the agent with a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.

rationale: Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not require, eliminating the attack surface rather than monitoring or guarding it. Logging (A) and confirmations (C) are detective/compensating controls, not removal of unnecessary privilege; model size (D) is unrelated to authorization scope.

question: An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message. Latency and cost are both concerns. Which optimization most directly addresses both?

options.A: Truncate the policy document to the first 1,000 tokens.
options.B: Switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit.
options.C: Place the static system prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enable prompt caching.
options.D: Move the policy document into a few-shot example block.

rationale: Ordering stable content first and enabling prompt caching lets repeated prefixes be reused, reducing both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context. Truncation (A) loses needed policy; downsizing blindly (B) risks quality; relocating to few-shot (D) does not create a cacheable, reusable prefix.

question: A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged. What is the most likely first place to investigate?

options.A: The model weights have silently changed.
options.B: The retrieval/indexing step is returning irrelevant or stale chunks.
options.C: The temperature setting is too low.
options.D: The context window has shrunk.

rationale: Confident-but-wrong answers following a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other options would not be triggered specifically by a document refresh.

question: A document-intake pipeline runs two Claude stages on the same model. Stage one routes about 400,000 incoming emails a day into one of six queues, using labels that human reviewers agree on almost without exception. Stage two drafts a monthly regulatory analysis that reasons across dozens of filings. Finance asks the architect to cut cost. Which recommendation is best?

options.A: Move both stages to the smallest model, since a single uniform tier keeps the pipeline simpler to operate
options.B: Keep both stages on the current model, since any model change risks quality regressions in production
options.C: Evaluate a smaller model on the routing stage against a labeled set and switch only if it meets the bar
options.D: Move the regulatory stage to a smaller model, since it runs only monthly and its volume is negligible

rationale: The cost sits in the high-volume routing stage, whose crisp labels make it the stage most likely to be served by a smaller model, and the switch is justified by evaluation rather than assumed. Moving everything down (A) ignores the deep reasoning stage two needs. Refusing any change (B) forgoes a saving the evidence may well support; model changes are managed with evaluation, not avoided. Downsizing the regulatory stage (D) targets the stage with negligible volume and the highest reasoning demand, saving little while risking the most.
evidence: Model selection is a cost-latency-quality tradeoff argued from the task, not brand preference.

question: A legal team's summarization assistant must cite sources in an in-house citation style with several irregular cases (consolidated dockets, sealed exhibits, superseded rulings). The summaries are accurate, but citations for the irregular cases come out inconsistent, and two rewrites of the prose description of the style have not helped. The team has a set of correctly cited documents. What should the architect change first?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the firm's past briefs so that the citation style is learned in the weights
options.B: Add worked examples of each irregular case to the prompt, then re-test on held-out documents
options.C: Expand the prose description of the style and mark the irregular-case rules as critical in capitals
options.D: Ask the model to reason step by step about each citation before it writes the final summary

rationale: A format that is hard to state in prose is best conveyed by demonstration: few-shot examples covering exactly the failing irregular cases, checked on documents that were not used as examples. Fine-tuning (A) is the slow, expensive answer to a problem that examples in the prompt already solve. More prose and emphasis (C) repeats the approach that has failed twice. Chain-of-thought (D) helps multi-step reasoning, but the failure is an unfamiliar output format, not a reasoning error, and more reasoning without a reference pattern does not show the model what the style looks like.
evidence: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

question: An account-research agent calls a CRM lookup tool six to eight times per task. Each call returns the full account record, about 15,000 tokens of history and metadata, although the agent only ever uses the contact name, account tier and renewal date. Long tasks now hit the context limit, and reasoning in the later steps degrades. Which change best addresses the problem?

options.A: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window so that all of the records fit
options.B: Enable prompt caching on the tool results so the repeated records cost less per call
options.C: Instruct the agent in its system prompt to ignore every record field it does not need
options.D: Have the tool return only the fields the task uses before results enter the context

rationale: The context is being spent on data the task never uses; trimming the tool's output at the source keeps each call to a few hundred tokens, which addresses both the limit and the dilution that degrades later reasoning. A larger window (A) delays the same failure at higher cost and leaves the irrelevant material in place. Caching (B) reuses a stable prefix to cut cost and latency, but it does not reduce how much of the window the records occupy. An instruction to ignore fields (C) still sends every token into the context, so neither the limit nor the dilution changes.
evidence: Optimize context windows and manage token usage

question: Twelve internal assistants each carry their own pasted copy of the same compliance disclaimer and escalation procedure in their system prompts. Legal revised the wording a month ago; four assistants still use the old text, and nobody can say which version each assistant was running last week. What should the architect put in place?

options.A: A single versioned module for the shared block, referenced by every assistant and reviewed on change
options.B: Prompt caching on each assistant's system prompt so the shared disclaimer is processed only once
options.C: A quarterly audit that compares every assistant's copy with legal's master text and fixes differences
options.D: One merged assistant to replace all twelve, so that only a single system prompt is left to maintain

rationale: The failure is duplicated prompt content drifting silently. Factoring the shared block into one versioned module that every assistant references means a change is made once, reviewed, and traceable to a version. Caching (B) is a cost and latency mechanism; it neither propagates new wording nor records which version ran. A quarterly audit (C) is a detective control that leaves assistants out of date for months. Merging the assistants (D) throws away their specialisation to solve a maintenance problem that modular prompts solve directly.
evidence: Prompt reuse at enterprise scale means modular prompts, versioning, and Skills, so behavior changes are reviewable events rather than silent drift.

question: A customer-service assistant looks up orders through a tool that accepts any order number. Its only protection is a system-prompt rule never to disclose other customers' orders. A red-team tester obtained another customer's delivery address by supplying that customer's order number with a plausible story. The product owner proposes rewording the rule more forcefully. What should the architect recommend instead?

options.A: Log every order lookup and have the support team review those logs weekly for suspicious access
options.B: Scope the lookup tool to the authenticated customer's orders and add an output check as a layer
options.C: Keep the reworded rule and move to a larger model that follows system instructions more reliably
options.D: Require customers to restate the order number twice before the assistant reveals any details

rationale: The prompt rule is a single layer, and it has already failed. Restricting the tool to the authenticated customer's own orders removes the capability that was abused, and an output check adds an independent layer behind it. Weekly log review (A) detects a leak after the data is gone. A stronger rule on a larger model (C) is still one bypassable prompt-level layer. Restating the number (D) does nothing against an attacker who already has it.
evidence: Layer guardrails: input validation, output filtering, scoped permissions, human-in-the-loop for consequential actions. One layer is a single point of failure.

question: A recruiting firm will use Claude to shortlist applicants for interview. Validated against recruiters' past decisions, the shortlister agrees 94% of the time overall, and the team has already removed names and photos from its inputs. Applicants are not currently told how shortlists are produced. Before launch, the ethics review asks for one more addition. Which is most important?

options.A: Senior recruiters reviewing a random sample of shortlists every week and correcting any poor picks
options.B: Also redacting universities and postcodes, since those fields can act as proxies for background
options.C: Raising agreement with recruiters' past decisions to 98% on a larger and more recent validation set
options.D: Comparing shortlist rates between applicant groups, and disclosing the model's role to candidates

rationale: Nothing yet measures whether outcomes differ between groups: a 94% aggregate can hide large gaps, and agreement with past recruiter decisions can simply reproduce their bias. Applicants are also unaware that a model is involved. Comparing outcomes across groups and disclosing the model's role closes both gaps. Weekly recruiter sampling (A) judges shortlists against the same recruiter standard that may carry the bias, and a random sample does not compare groups. Redacting more fields (B) is a sensible mitigation, but like the first redaction it is unmeasured, so nobody can tell whether a disparity remains. A higher agreement target (C) is still an aggregate tied to past decisions, so closer agreement can mean closer reproduction of past bias.
evidence: Ethics is scored concretely: bias testing, fairness across user groups, transparency about AI involvement.

question: A US federal agency plans a cloud-hosted Claude assistant to help its caseworkers answer benefit inquiries. Some inquiries include applicants' medical details, and a small share come from applicants living in the EU. The agency CIO asks which regulatory consideration decides which hosting environments the solution may use at all. Which answer is best?

options.A: HIPAA, since medical details in the inquiries must be de-identified before they leave the agency
options.B: GDPR, since applicants in the EU mean the service has to be hosted in an EU region to serve them
options.C: FedRAMP, since a federal agency may only deploy to cloud services authorized for federal use
options.D: The agency's records-retention schedule, since every transcript must be kept for a set period

rationale: The question is which environments the agency may deploy to at all, and for a US federal agency's cloud deployment that is what FedRAMP governs: authorized environments carrying the required controls. HIPAA (A) is relevant to how health information flows through the design, but it is a data-handling obligation, not the rule that determines which cloud environments a federal agency may use. GDPR (B) is about how personal data of people in the EU is processed (minimization, purpose limitation, erasure) and touches only a small share of inquiries; it does not decide the agency's hosting environment. A retention schedule (D) shapes what is stored and for how long, not where the solution may run.
evidence: US federal cloud deployments: authorized environments and controls

question: At kickoff, an insurer's COO says, "We want a Claude agent for claims." The engineering team, keen to show momentum, proposes building a multi-agent prototype over the next two weeks. Nobody has yet said which part of claims handling is costly, what constraints apply, or how success would be measured. What should the architect do first?

options.A: Run structured discovery on the problem, constraints and success measures before choosing a design
options.B: Build the prototype quickly, since a working demo is the fastest way to surface the real requirements
options.C: Choose the model and orchestration framework first, since those choices constrain every later decision
options.D: Request all historical claims data so the team can explore it and find where an agent would add value

rationale: With no stated problem, constraints or success measure, any design, including the choice of an agent at all, is a guess. Discovery comes before architecture. A prototype (B) commits to a multi-agent design before anyone knows whether the problem needs one, and its demo cannot be judged without success measures. Picking the model and framework (C) is a design decision taken before the requirement exists. A bulk data request (D) is exploration without a question, and it raises data-handling obligations before any purpose has been established.
evidence: Structured discovery before design: business problem, constraints, success measures, then architecture.

question: Three months after launch, business users of a contract-review assistant keep reporting that it is "too slow". Requests range from quick clause lookups to full reviews of 80-page agreements, and no response-time target was ever agreed for either. The team has made several tuning changes, and after each one the complaints continue. What should the architect do next?

options.A: Move full reviews to a faster model once an evaluation confirms that review quality is maintained
options.B: Enable streaming so text appears sooner, then survey users after a month on whether it feels faster
options.C: Add per-request latency dashboards so the team can see exactly where the time is being spent
options.D: Agree with the business how fast each kind of request must be, then track and report against that

rationale: The complaints persist because nobody has defined fast enough for either kind of request, so no change can be shown to have succeeded. Agreeing a target per request type with the business, then measuring and reporting against it, turns the complaint into a shared, testable expectation. A faster model (A) is a reasonable lever, but without a target nobody knows whether the result will be fast enough or whether the lookups were the problem. Streaming plus a survey (B) improves perceived speed and gathers opinions, but it still leaves no agreed threshold to judge against. Dashboards (C) show where time goes inside the team, but they do not tell the team what speed the business expects.
evidence: expectations get managed with explicit SLAs

question: A Claude solution was handed over to a client's platform team, which now owns it and must evolve it independently. The handoff package was a complete set of architecture diagrams. Within a month the team moved a per-user greeting to the top of the system prompt, which broke prompt caching and raised costs, and removed a validation step they believed was redundant. Neither change contradicted the diagrams. What should future handoffs add?

options.A: Diagrams annotated with every prompt section and pipeline step, kept current in the client's wiki
options.B: A written account of why each design choice was made and the constraints any change must respect
options.C: A hands-on session walking the client team through how to operate and deploy each component
options.D: A sign-off step in which the architect's team reviews every prompt or pipeline edit before release

rationale: Both changes were reasonable-looking edits that broke an unstated constraint: static content goes first so caching works, and the validation step is a guardrail. What the client lacked was the reasoning behind the design, so handoff must carry the reasons and the constraints that later changes have to respect. Annotated diagrams (A) record more of what was built, but the edits did not contradict the diagrams, so more detail on structure would not have prevented them. An operations walkthrough (C) teaches how to run and deploy the system, not why it is built the way it is. Architect sign-off (D) catches errors only by keeping the original team in the loop, which contradicts the requirement that the client evolve the solution independently.
evidence: handoff includes implementation guidance, not just diagrams
